bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 13: Text classification and Naive Bayes
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, April 1 2009 draft)

question: How can a repetitive filtering task be automated as text classification, and how well do Naive Bayes classifiers, feature selection and standard evaluation measures work for it?
contributions: Defines the text classification problem and contrasts hand rules with learned classifiers
Derives multinomial and Bernoulli NB with add-one smoothing and worked examples
Explains why NB classifies well despite poor probability estimates
Covers feature selection by mutual information, chi-square and frequency
Covers evaluation: micro/macro averaging, Reuters-21578 ModApte benchmark, held-out protocol

limits: Dated: comparisons use Reuters-21578 with 2003 and 1998 results (NB, Rocchio, kNN, trees, SVM); no neural or embedding-based classifiers, no pretrained language models.
Feature-selection experiments (Fig 13.8) are read from a plotted figure with no numeric table; averaged over five classes only and one train/test split.
Table 13.9 parts (a) and (b) come from different papers with different metrics (true F1 over 90 classes vs break-even over 118 classes); the authors concede they are not comparable.
Authors concede the independence assumptions do not hold for text; NB probability estimates are of low quality.
Chi-square selection is statistically problematic (no Yates correction, multiple testing) and all three selectors are greedy and can pick redundant terms (kong after hong).
Many numbers in Table 13.9 are quoted second-hand and not reproduced here.
practices: Compute NB in log space (sum of log prior and log conditionals) to avoid floating-point underflow (p.258-259).
Use add-one (Laplace) smoothing so a term unseen in a class does not zero the class score (p.260).
Estimate class priors from document counts, not token counts (Fig 13.2, Exercise 13.7).
Use the multinomial model for longer documents and many features; use the Bernoulli model for short documents and few features, and always with feature selection (Table 13.3, p.272).
Select features by mutual information or chi-square; frequency selection is acceptable only when many thousands of features are kept (p.277-278).
Prefer NB when a few extra accuracy points are not worth the effort, when very large training data is available, or when robustness to concept drift matters (p.270).
For small classes use precision, recall and F1, not accuracy; report macro-averages to see small-class behaviour and micro-averages for large-class behaviour (p.280-281).
Keep the test set untouched: tune parameters such as number of features on a development or held-out set, and run one final test experiment (p.283-284).
With many classifiers, use one shared feature set only if efficiency is worth a possible accuracy loss (p.278).

terms.definition: A query that is periodically executed on a collection to which new documents are incrementally added over time.
A probabilistic learning method where P(c|d) is proportional to P(c) times the product over token positions of P(tk|c).
Generates a binary presence/absence indicator for each vocabulary term; equivalent to the binary independence model.
Attribute values are independent of each other given the class.
The conditional probabilities for a term are the same independent of position in the document; equivalent to bag of words.
A feature that, when added to the document representation, increases the classification error on new data.
The gradual change over time of the concept underlying a class.
A simple average of the effectiveness measure over classes.
Pools per-document decisions across classes, then computes the measure on the pooled contingency table.
A development set whose primary purpose is finding a good value for a parameter such as the number of selected features.
